exercises.prompt: Implement add(a, b) so it returns the sum of the two numbers a and b.
exercises.solution:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
hints: A Python function hands a value back only with the return keyword — an untouched stub runs pass and returns None, so every test fails.
The + operator adds two numbers: a + b.
The whole body is one line: return a + b (delete the pass).

exercises.prompt: Implement biggest(a, b) so it returns the larger of the two numbers. If they are equal, return that shared value.
exercises.solution:
def biggest(a, b):
    return a if a > b else b
hints: Compare the two values with the greater-than operator: a > b.
Python's conditional expression a if a > b else b evaluates to a when a is bigger and b otherwise — a one-line if/else.
When a and b are equal, a > b is False, so the expression returns b (which equals a) — the right shared value.

exercises.prompt: Implement fizzbuzz(n). Return 'Fizz' if n is divisible by 3, 'Buzz' if divisible by 5, 'FizzBuzz' if divisible by both, and otherwise the number itself as a string — fizzbuzz(7) returns '7'.
hints: The remainder operator % tells you divisibility: n % 3 == 0 is True exactly when n is a multiple of 3.
Check the both-divisible case first — n % 15 == 0 — otherwise 15 matches 'Fizz' and returns before reaching 'FizzBuzz'.
For the fall-through case, convert the number to text with str(n) so you return '7', not the integer 7.

exercises.prompt: Implement next_multiple(n, k) so it returns the smallest multiple of k that is greater than or equal to n — next_multiple(11, 5) is 15. When n is already a multiple of k, return n unchanged: next_multiple(10, 5) is 10 and next_multiple(0, 7) is 0. Assume n is zero or positive and k is a positive integer.
exercises.solution:
def next_multiple(n, k):
    return n if n % k == 0 else n + k - n % k
hints: The remainder n % k says how far n sits past the previous multiple of k — and a remainder of 0 means n is already a multiple, so it is its own answer.
When the remainder is not 0, you still have k - n % k to climb, which puts the answer at n + k - n % k.
Fold the two cases into one conditional expression: return n if n % k == 0 else n + k - n % k — adding the gap unconditionally would push an exact multiple a whole k too far.

exercises.prompt: Implement score_line(name, score) so it returns a sentence: the name, then ' scored ', then the score, then ' point' when the score is exactly 1 and ' points' for every other score. score_line('Ann', 3) is 'Ann scored 3 points', score_line('Bo', 1) is 'Bo scored 1 point', and score_line('Dee', -1) is 'Dee scored -1 points'. The result is always a string.
exercises.solution:
def score_line(name, score):
    return name + ' scored ' + str(score) + (' point' if score == 1 else ' points')
hints: You are gluing text together in four pieces: the name, a fixed middle, the score itself, and an ending that depends on the score.
A number cannot be joined to text as-is — str(score) turns 3 into '3' — and the conditional expression ' point' if score == 1 else ' points' picks the ending.
return name + ' scored ' + str(score) + (' point' if score == 1 else ' points') — only a score of exactly 1 is singular, so 0 and -1 both take ' points'.
